# Hello World

An over engineered Hello World! The program prints `HELLO WORLD!` five times, each in a different way. Not all of them are the right way to do it, but each one shows off a different BitMagic feature.

## How to run it

Open the folder in VSCode and press `F5`. The project has `autobootRun` set, so the program runs as soon as the emulator starts and you'll see the message five times.

The project also has `saveGeneratedBmasm` and `saveGeneratedTemplate` set, so after a build you can look in the `bin` folder to see exactly what the C# in `src/main.bmasm` turned into.

## The string

The text is a C# constant at the top of the file, so every method uses the same value:

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">const</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> string</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> hello_world_string </span><span style="color:#B5E853">=</span><span style="color:#E6DB74"> "HELLO WORLD!\r\n"</span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">;</span></span></code></pre>

At the end of the file it's converted to PETSCII and written out as data. `BM.Bytes` adds a null terminator by default.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">.hello_world:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">    BM.Bytes(BM.StringToPetscii(hello_world_string))</span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">;</span></span></code></pre>

## The five methods

### 1. Indexed loop

`bsout_indexed` is the standard approach: index through the string with `x` and call `BSOUT` until it reaches the null terminator.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    ldx</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> #</span><span style="color:#FF79C6">0</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">.loop:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    lda</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> hello_world, x</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    beq</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> done</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jsr</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> BSOUT</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    inx</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jmp</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> loop</span></span></code></pre>

### 2. Self modifying code

`bsout_selfmodifying` isn't the best way to print a string, but it shows two things:

- A label inside an instruction. `read_address` points at the operand of the `lda`, so the code can change the address it reads from.
- Anonymous labels. `.:` defines one, and `+` and `-` jump to the next or previous one.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">.:  </span><span style="color:#B5E853">lda</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> read_address: </span><span style="color:#FF79C6">$1234</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    beq</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> +</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jsr</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> BSOUT</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    inc</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> read_address</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    bne</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> -</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    inc</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> read_address </span><span style="color:#B5E853">+</span><span style="color:#FF79C6"> 1</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jmp</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> -</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">.:  </span><span style="color:#B5E853">rts</span></span></code></pre>

### 3. Length from C#

`bsout_indexed_macro` uses a C# expression to get the length of the string at compile time, so it doesn't need the null terminator. `@(...)` puts the result of any C# expression into the assembly.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    ldx</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> #</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA">@(hello_world_string.Length)    </span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">; ldx #14</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    ldy</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> #</span><span style="color:#FF79C6">0</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">.:  </span><span style="color:#B5E853">lda</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> hello_world, y</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jsr</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> BSOUT</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    iny</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    dex</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    bne</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> -</span></span></code></pre>

### 4. Unrolled loop

`bsout_unrolled` uses a C# `for` loop to write out an `lda` and `jsr BSOUT` for every character. There's no loop at runtime and no data block, just straight line code.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    var</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> toDisplay </span><span style="color:#B5E853">=</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> BM.StringToPetscii(hello_world_string).ToArray()</span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">;</span></span>
<span class="line"></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    for</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA">(</span><span style="color:#B5E853">var</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> i </span><span style="color:#B5E853">=</span><span style="color:#FF79C6"> 0</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA">; i </span><span style="color:#B5E853">&#x3C;</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> toDisplay.Length; i</span><span style="color:#B5E853">++</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA">)</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">        lda</span><span style="color:#B5E853"> #</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA">@(toDisplay[i])</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">        jsr</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> BSOUT</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">    }</span></span></code></pre>

The generated `.bmasm` in the `bin` folder shows the 14 pairs of instructions this produces.

### 5. PRIMM

`primm` calls the kernal's `PRIMM`, which prints the null terminated string that directly follows the `jsr`, then returns to the instruction after it. The string is placed inline with `BM.Bytes`. The code selects the kernal ROM bank (bank 0) before the call and restores the previous bank afterwards.

<pre class="shiki"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    lda</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> ROM_BANK</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    pha</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    stz</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> ROM_BANK        </span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">; kernal ROM bank</span></span>
<span class="line"></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    jsr</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> PRIMM</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#EAEAEA">    BM.Bytes(BM.StringToPetscii(hello_world_string))</span><span style="color:#8F8F8F;font-style:italic">;</span></span>
<span class="line"></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    pla</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#B5E853">    sta</span><span style="color:#EAEAEA"> ROM_BANK</span></span></code></pre>
